analysis.one_liner: Orders the futures regulator to curb excessive oil speculation and set strict trading limits in energy markets.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote; it died in the House Agriculture Committee after its single referral, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, within 14 days of becoming law, to use its powers, including emergency powers, to curb excessive speculation in energy futures markets and to finalize and enforce limits on how large any single trader's positions can be. Its stated aim was to stop Wall Street trading from pushing gasoline and oil prices above what supply and demand would set. It was introduced by one representative, sent to the House Agriculture Committee, and never received any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that buy gasoline, diesel, and heating fuel, who the bill's findings say were paying a speculator-driven premium at the pump. The bill cites an estimate that excessive oil speculation added about 56 cents to a gallon of gasoline, and notes gas hit a record March average of over $3.94 a gallon in 2012 even though oil supply was up and U.S. gasoline demand was at 1998 levels.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the CFTC, within 14 days of enactment, to immediately curb the role of excessive speculation in any market trading energy futures or swaps, using its authority including emergency powers.
Requires the CFTC to eliminate price distortion, sudden or unreasonable fluctuations, and unwarranted price changes caused by excessive speculation, so energy prices reflect actual supply and demand.
Requires the CFTC to prioritize finalizing and enforcing a position limits regime, capping how large a stake any single trader can build in energy markets.

The bill's findings cite CFTC Chairman Gary Gensler's 2011 testimony that 80 to 87 percent of the oil futures market was held by financial players such as swap dealers and hedge funds, a share that had more than doubled in a decade.

analysis.who_pays: Financial firms that trade energy futures and swaps for profit, including hedge funds, swap dealers, and the commodity trading desks of large banks, which would face immediate curbs and hard position limits. Commodity exchanges would also face closer control over their energy contracts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hedge funds and bank commodity desks

drawbacks.text: The link between speculation and pump prices is contested; the 56-cents-a-gallon figure the bill cites comes from a single Forbes article reporting a Goldman Sachs estimate, and many economists argue supply, demand, and world events set oil prices more than futures trading does.

Aggressive, hastily imposed position limits within 14 days could reduce market liquidity and make it harder for legitimate hedgers, such as airlines, trucking firms, and oil producers, to lock in fuel costs, raising costs for some of the same consumers the bill aims to help.
The 14-day deadline gives the regulator almost no time for analysis or public comment before upending energy trading markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If speculation does inflate pump prices, the bill targeted a real cost that hits every driver and business, and position limits were a policy the CFTC was already required to write under the 2010 financial reform law. But the bill's hard evidence rests on a contested estimate, and its 14-day deadline was blunt enough to risk disrupting markets that airlines and farmers rely on for hedging. The upside for consumers was plausible but uncertain; the design was rushed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee, then to a subcommittee, and neither ever took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Representative Kathleen Hochul introduced the bill on April 18, 2012, with no cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Agriculture Committee the same day, and on May 10, 2012, to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management.
No hearing, markup, vote, or further action of any kind appears in the action history, and the bill died at the end of the 112th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial firms that trade energy futures, including hedge funds, swap dealers, and bank commodity desks, kept trading without the immediate curbs and position limits the bill would have imposed. The House Agriculture Committee, whose jurisdiction covers futures markets, faced no requirement to act.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Energy futures traders and hedge funds

for.name: Rep. Kathleen Hochul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require the CFTC to curb excessive energy speculation and enforce position limits.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over futures markets
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 18, 2012, and sent it to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management on May 10, 2012, but never held a markup or vote, letting the bill expire.

against.name: Frank Lucas
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee action; it sat in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and no other member cosponsored the bill, so the record shows only where its Democratic sponsor stood, not where the parties as a whole stood.

industries.industry: Energy futures traders (hedge funds, swap dealers, bank commodity desks)
industries.note: The bill would have immediately curbed their trading and imposed position limits within 14 days. Their gain from the bill's death was the continued ability to hold large speculative positions in oil and gasoline markets.

The CFTC would have had to police speculative activity on every market trading energy futures, tightening oversight of their core business. Tighter limits could also cut trading volume, a direct cost to exchanges.

Producers hedge with futures, and blunt 14-day limits could have complicated that. But if speculation was inflating prices above supply-and-demand levels, the bill aimed to bring prices closer to fundamentals, which affects revenue in both directions.
